title: Integrating artificial intelligence into science lessons: teachers’ experiences and views
extended_summary:
This paper examines how science teachers experienced and perceived the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) content into regular lower-secondary science instruction. The central problem is how to introduce AI in schools without treating it as a stand-alone subject, especially when most teachers are not formally trained in AI and must integrate it into existing disciplinary curricula. The study asks how teachers perceived the relationship between AI and science, what implementation challenges they encountered, and what improvements they recommended after piloting an AI-integrated science lesson package.

The intervention was a researcher-designed AI-integrated science lesson package aligned with Singapore’s Grade 7 lower secondary science curriculum, specifically the theme of models. The package included pre-lesson video primers on AI and machine learning, review of key science ideas, activities linking science and AI concepts, and a hands-on predictive-modeling task using the Orange software. Students used Mars Rover data to build and test predictive models related to conditions for deploying solar panels on Mars. The approach was explicitly discipline-focused: AI was introduced as a tool for scientific modeling and problem-solving rather than as a separate computing topic.

Participants were three science teachers from three different secondary schools in Singapore and their 37 Grade 7 students. The lessons were implemented after school as a 3-hour session. Data came from teacher reflection sessions, classroom observations, lesson audio/video recordings, field notes, and student worksheets. The study used an instrumental case study approach with qualitative analysis focused on teachers’ views of AI-science connections, implementation barriers, and suggested revisions.

The main conclusions were that teachers saw meaningful overlap between AI and science in model-building, data use, and simplified reasoning, but also viewed the two as playing complementary roles: science provided contextual understanding and judgment about relevant variables, while AI functioned as a tool for generating predictions from large datasets. The biggest implementation challenge was teachers’ lack of confidence in their own AI content mastery, especially regarding machine-learning mechanisms. Teachers also anticipated barriers to broader adoption, including limited teacher buy-in, curriculum adaptation demands, and concerns about targeting the right student audience. They recommended more comprehensive teacher resources and suggested the package may be better suited for after-school enrichment contexts unless stronger supports are provided.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed qualitative instrumental case study with classroom observation, teacher reflection, and student worksheet evidence, but no experimental design, no validated outcome measures, and no causal identification strategy. It therefore fits yellow under the framework as a qualitative study with limited credibility for effectiveness claims.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially useful but unclear impacts: students may have learned aspects of scientific modeling/AI integration, while implementation feasibility was constrained. Because outcomes are qualitative and effect sizes are absent, overall impact is best classified as unclear rather than clearly positive or negative.

interventions.use_case: Teacher-facilitated AI-integrated Grade 7 science lesson package using pre-lesson videos, Google Quick Draw, and the Orange software to help small groups build a predictive model about Mars solar-panel deployment as part of AI literacy/science integration.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports qualitative evidence that teachers believed the lesson package helped students connect scientific modeling with AI/ML, especially around using data to build and refine predictive models. Observationally, most students appeared to grasp the broad workflow of model training and testing, and 32 of 37 students reportedly answered a worksheet question correctly about which dataset produced the most accurate prediction; however, no validated pre/post assessment, control group, or effect size was reported, so impact on scientific reasoning remains suggestive rather than causal.
finding.measure: Teacher reflections, classroom observations, student worksheets on predictive-model selection and understanding of data/model relationships

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that implementing the AI-integrated lesson package was challenging because of low confidence in their own AI content mastery and difficulty adapting curriculum within regular instruction. They recommended stronger teacher resources and suggested the package may fit better in after-school enrichment contexts, indicating implementation burden and feasibility constraints rather than demonstrated classroom efficiency gains.
finding.measure: Teacher interview/reflection reports on implementation challenges, preparedness, and feasibility

finding.finding_summary: The study found that teachers saw conceptual value in integrating AI into science, but anticipated barriers to broader adoption, including lack of teacher buy-in, curriculum adaptation pressures, and uncertainty about the appropriate student audience. Their recommendation to position the package within enrichment or after-school programs suggests partial institutional fit but limited readiness for routine whole-curriculum uptake.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of curriculum fit, adoption barriers, and recommendations for school implementation

finding.finding_summary: The lesson package was designed around collaborative, inquiry-oriented small-group problem solving, and teacher reflections suggested students engaged in reasoning about relevant versus irrelevant variables, model improvement, and problem solving with data. However, these outcomes were inferred from classroom interaction and worksheet performance rather than measured with validated collaboration, critical thinking, or metacognitive instruments.
finding.measure: Observed collaborative inquiry activity, teacher reflections, worksheet-based reasoning about variables and prediction
